title: LLC vs S Corp for Real Estate Investors: Which Is Better in 2025?
excerpt: Choosing between an LLC and an S corp can save real estate investors thousands in taxes every year. This guide breaks down the key differences, pros, cons, and exactly when each structure makes sense for your investing business.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: LLC vs S corp real estate investors
metaDescription: LLC vs S corp for real estate investors: compare taxes, liability, and structure to choose the best entity for your investing business in 2025.

sections.content: One of the most common questions new and growing real estate investors ask is: should I form an LLC or an S corp? It sounds like a simple question, but the answer can have a major impact on how much you pay in taxes, how protected your personal assets are, and how smoothly your business runs. If you are serious about building a long-term investing business, getting this decision right early can save you tens of thousands of dollars. For a full picture of what it takes to grow, check out the [Scaling a Real Estate Investing Business: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/scaling-real-estate-investing-business) — entity structure is one of the first pillars you need to get right.
Understanding the Basics: LLC vs S Corp

First, let's clear up a common misconception. An S corporation is not a type of business entity — it is a tax election. An LLC (Limited Liability Company) is an actual legal entity. You can form an LLC and then elect to have it taxed as an S corp with the IRS. This means you are not always choosing one over the other. Sometimes, the smartest move is to combine both. Still, each approach comes with its own rules, costs, and tax treatment, so understanding the differences is essential.
What Is an LLC?

An LLC is a flexible legal structure that gives you personal liability protection while keeping administration simple. For real estate investors, this is the most popular starting point. If you own a rental property or flip houses through an LLC and a tenant sues you, your personal bank accounts and home are generally protected. By default, a single-member LLC is taxed as a sole proprietorship, and a multi-member LLC is taxed as a partnership. All profits flow through to your personal tax return, and you pay self-employment taxes on net income — which is 15.3% on the first $160,200 as of 2024.
What Is an S Corp?

An S corp is a tax designation you file for with the IRS using Form 2553. When your LLC is taxed as an S corp, you split your income into two buckets: a reasonable salary you pay yourself as a W-2 employee, and distributions. You only pay self-employment taxes on the salary portion — not on the distributions. This is where the big tax savings come in for active real estate businesses. If your LLC generates $150,000 in net profit and you pay yourself a $60,000 salary, you only owe self-employment tax on $60,000 instead of the full $150,000. That can save you roughly $13,770 per year.
When an LLC Makes More Sense

For investors who are just getting started or primarily hold rental properties, a standard LLC is usually the better choice. Rentals generate passive income, which is already exempt from self-employment tax regardless of your entity structure. Adding an S corp election on top of a rental portfolio creates more paperwork, payroll costs, and accounting fees without much tax benefit. If you are exploring real estate for the first time, the [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) gives a great overview before you dive into advanced tax strategies.

items: You hold long-term rental properties with passive income
Your net profit from active deals is below $40,000 to $50,000 per year
You want to minimize administrative costs and payroll complexity
You are investing part-time and do not yet take a salary from the business
You own properties in multiple states and want clean liability separation between assets

sections.content: When an S Corp Election Pays Off

The S corp election starts to make sense when your real estate business generates consistent active income above $50,000 per year. This is most common for wholesalers, house flippers, and full-time investors doing multiple deals. Once your profits cross that threshold, the self-employment tax savings will outweigh the added cost of running payroll, filing an additional tax return (Form 1120-S), and potentially hiring an accountant. Most CPAs recommend switching when net active income hits $50,000 to $80,000 annually.

items: You wholesale or flip houses and generate active, earned income
Net profit from active deals exceeds $50,000 per year consistently
You are already paying yourself and want to reduce self-employment tax legally
You have [built SOPs for your real estate business](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/sops-real-estate-business) and are operating like a real company
You are hiring team members like an acquisitions manager or transaction coordinator

sections.content: Pro Tip: Talk to a CPA before making the S corp election. The IRS requires you to pay yourself a 'reasonable salary' — and if that salary is too low, you could face an audit. A common benchmark is paying yourself 40% to 60% of your net profit as salary and taking the rest as a distribution.
Real-World Example: Wholesaler Saving with an S Corp

Let's say you are a wholesaler operating in a competitive market like [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga) or [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx). You close 20 wholesale deals a year with an average assignment fee of $8,000, generating $160,000 in gross revenue. After expenses, your net profit is $100,000. As a standard LLC, you pay self-employment tax of roughly $14,130 (after deductions) on top of your income tax. With an S corp election and a $55,000 reasonable salary, your SE tax drops to about $7,771 — saving you over $6,000 per year. Over five years, that is $30,000 back in your pocket, minus roughly $2,000 to $3,000 per year for added accounting fees. The math clearly favors the S corp at that income level.

'The best entity structure is the one that matches where your business is today — not where you hope it will be. Start simple, optimize as you grow.' — Common advice from real estate CPAs specializing in investor tax strategy
The LLC + S Corp Combination Strategy

Many experienced investors use both structures simultaneously. They hold rental properties inside one or more standard LLCs for liability protection and passive income benefits. Then they run their active business — flipping, wholesaling, or property management — through a separate LLC that has elected S corp tax treatment. This separation also makes it easier to bring on partners, track income by deal type, and protect assets. If you are growing your team and scaling up, knowing [when to hire an acquisitions manager](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/acquisitions-manager-real-estate) is another important decision that often coincides with the right time to restructure your entities.
Key Administrative Differences to Know

items: S corps must run payroll and file quarterly payroll tax returns (Form 941)
S corps require an annual corporate tax return (Form 1120-S) separate from your personal return
S corps cannot have more than 100 shareholders or non-US citizen owners
LLCs have no ownership restrictions and fewer filing requirements
Both structures require separate business bank accounts and clean bookkeeping
Annual state fees apply to both, but vary widely by state — from $0 in Wyoming to $800+ in California

sections.content: Active Markets and Entity Strategy

Where you invest can also influence your entity strategy. Some states have higher franchise taxes or additional fees that make S corps more expensive. For example, California charges an $800 minimum franchise tax on LLCs regardless of income, plus a gross receipts fee. Investors working in high-volume markets like [Phoenix, AZ](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) or [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) often find the S corp savings far outweigh state fees. Always factor in your state's specific costs before making the election. A local real estate CPA can run the exact numbers for your situation.

Whether you are running a lean wholesaling operation or scaling a full acquisition machine, your entity structure should align with your deal volume, revenue, and growth plan. As you add team members and refine your [disposition strategies to move wholesale deals faster](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/wholesale-disposition-strategies), the administrative structure of your business needs to keep up.
